options.why: No such division is drawn. Taking in information and producing an output are steps of the same described system.

options.text: The brackets show which steps have been solved, leaving the others as open problems.
options.why: Nothing in the figure marks any step as settled, and neither central question is presented as answered.

items.stem: The chapter says most brain and cognitive scientists describe the mind in the language of computation, and then immediately says the position is contested. Why does stating the first make stating the second more important rather than less?

options.text: A prevailing description is the one most likely to be mistaken for a settled finding.
options.why: Correct. The move mirrors the earlier honesty about whether the field is one subject. A reader meeting a vocabulary used by nearly everyone will assume the argument for it was won; saying plainly that it was not is what keeps the lens from hardening into a doctrine.

options.text: Widely held positions are more often wrong than positions held by a minority.
options.why: No such claim is made, and the chapter's case for the computational description is a strong one it goes on to use.

options.text: The disagreement is confined to a few specialists, so it would otherwise go unmentioned.
options.why: The objections are presented as serious and from serious people, not as a marginal complaint.

options.text: Being contested is what makes a description scientific rather than merely conventional.
options.why: Contestedness is reported as a fact about this position rather than offered as a criterion for anything.

items.stem: Opening the computational material in lecture, the instructor warned that one word gets used two completely different ways in this field and that people conflate them constantly. What are the two?

options.text: A claim about what a mind is, and a claim about how scientists go about studying minds.
options.why: Correct. The lecture separates them before saying anything else about either, on the grounds that running them together is a standing source of confusion. The chapter makes both points but does not warn that they are routinely mixed up.

options.text: A claim about the mind and a separate claim about the brain that supports it.
options.why: Both senses are about the mind. What differs is whether the word describes the subject or the method used to study it.

options.text: A precise technical definition and a looser everyday usage of the same term.
options.why: The two senses are not degrees of precision. Each is definite; they are simply about different things.

options.text: The version used about human minds and the version used about artificial systems.
options.why: Neither sense is restricted by what kind of system is being described; the point of the description is that it spans them.

items.stem: Introducing representation and processing in lecture as the field's names for the two central questions, the instructor attached a flag to one of them. What was it?

options.text: Exactly what the term representation commits one to is itself argued about, and gets sharpened later.
options.why: Correct. The instructor adopts the word and uses it every week while marking that its content is disputed — which is why the pair can be learned and used before that dispute is anywhere near settled.

options.text: Neither term has a settled definition yet, so both should be treated as provisional.
options.why: Only one of the two was flagged, and both were given as terms to write down and use throughout.

options.text: The two questions are really one question asked from opposite directions.
options.why: They were presented as genuinely distinct, dividing the middle of the process between them.

options.text: The term representation in particular is borrowed from computer science and fits living minds only loosely.
options.why: Their origin was not the point raised, and the flag concerned what the word commits one to rather than where it came from.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why leaving out what a system is physically made of is presented as the deepest reason for describing minds computationally, rather than as a weakness of the description.
items.answer: The systems the book wants to hold in view — a person, a bee, an octopus, a machine — share almost nothing in what they are made of. Any description that mentioned the material would therefore fit one of them and fail for the rest: talk of neurons excludes the machine, talk of silicon excludes the animals. A computational description mentions neither. It says only that information comes in, is held in some internal form, is transformed, and issues in an output, and all four systems can be described that way without strain. So the omission is not a gap left by an incomplete account; it is what makes the account general enough to do the job the field needs done. The material is not being denied or treated as unimportant — it is the subject of a different question, and one this book keeps asking. What the omission buys is a single vocabulary in which the four cases can be compared at all.
rubric: States that the systems in question share almost nothing physically.
Explains that any material-mentioning description would fit some cases and not others.
Says what the computational description does mention instead — information, its internal form, transformation, output.
Draws the conclusion that the omission is what makes one account cover all the cases.
Notes that leaving the material out is not denying its importance, only asking a different question.

items.stem: A friend calls your name from across a room and you turn around. In a few sentences, say what the questions of representation and of processing each ask about that moment, and give one example of what an answer to each might look like.
items.answer: Representation asks what form the information is held in at each stage between the eardrum and the turn. An answer might say that the pressure wave is held first as speech sounds, then as words, then as a speaker and a meaning — three different forms of the same information, each further from the physical signal. Processing asks what turns one of those forms into the next: what operation takes a pattern of speech sounds and yields a word, and what takes a word plus a voice and yields the recognition that a particular person wants your attention. The two questions need each other. Naming the forms says nothing about how the mind gets from one to the next, and describing an operation presupposes something for it to operate on.
rubric: Says representation asks what form the information is held in.
Says processing asks what transforms one form into another, or turns input into output.
Gives at least one concrete form the information takes in this example.
Gives at least one concrete transformation between stages.
Notes that the two questions are distinct but interdependent.
